sessions.setting: At their shared raised bed in the Eastside Community Garden on a Saturday morning

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Morning, Sam! The Cherokee Purples are looking strong this year. I think the compost we added in February really made a difference.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Morning, Ruth. Yeah, they're way ahead of last year. How many tomato varieties do we have going in this bed now?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Fourteen, if you count the ones I started from seed in January. Cherokee Purple, Brandywine, a few others. This twenty-by-forty bed gives us just enough room.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: It's wild that we share this whole raised bed and still find room for everything. Speaking of room, my Carolina Reapers are coming in hot over in my personal plot. Literally.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: I saw those! And the habaneros too. Sam, you're going to burn a hole through the earth with those peppers.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ha! My grandmother Lupe would be proud. Hey, I was thinking about the garden's history the other day. How long has this place been going now?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: We started it in 2018. Got a five-thousand-dollar grant from the Austin Parks Foundation to get the Cesar Chavez Street lot set up. Feels like yesterday, honestly.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Six years already. You co-founded this whole thing and now look at it — must be thirty plots going.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Thirty-two! And every single one is spoken for. That's the best part — people actually want to be here.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: For sure. Oh, before I forget, do you need me to check on the drip lines this week? I noticed one of the emitters near the Brandywines was clogged.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: That would be wonderful. I'm going to be out here anyway checking on the bees later this afternoon. I'll save you some of my pepper soup from today if you come by.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: You don't even have to ask twice. Your Saturday pepper soup is the highlight of my week.

sessions.setting: Sunday morning at Bennu Coffee on East 11th Street

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Hey Hana! Grabbed you an oat milk latte — our usual Sunday planning session fuel.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You're the best, Sam. I really needed this. I've been running on fumes this week with my thesis.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: How's it going? You're in your second year of the urban planning master's at UT, right? Getting close to the finish line?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Getting there. I just wrapped up a survey of a hundred and fifty East Austin residents about green space access. The data is incredible — our garden keeps coming up as a positive example.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: No kidding! That's awesome. What's the thesis title again? Something about neighborhood resilience?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Yeah — 'Community-Led Green Spaces as Catalysts for Neighborhood Resilience in East Austin.' It's a mouthful, but my advisor loves it.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: It's perfect. So what's on the garden agenda for this week?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: We need to get the spring planting schedule finalized. I updated the garden app with everyone's plot assignments. Also, the herb section needs weeding badly.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: I can handle the weeding on Tuesday after school. What about the composting station?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Jenny said she'd turn the pile on Wednesday. And Ruth wants to start her second wave of tomato seedlings. Can you coordinate with her on the shared bed?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Already texted her about it. We're planning to put in the second round next Saturday.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Perfect. I love these Sunday planning sessions — keeps everything from falling through the cracks.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Same. Bennu Coffee and garden logistics — name a better combo.

sessions.setting: Chatting over the shared fence between their houses on East 6th Street

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Hana! You're up early. I just got back from my run around Lady Bird Lake.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You go every morning? I can barely get out of bed before eight.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Six fifteen, rain or shine. Three miles around the lake — it clears my head before I open the clinic. Being neighbors makes it nice, though. I get to say hi to you on the way out sometimes.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: The perks of sharing a fence, right? Hey, I noticed you've been running more lately. Training for something?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Actually, yes! I'm training for the Austin Marathon next February. It'll be my first full marathon. I figured if I start now, I'll have almost a year to build up.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: That's amazing, Jenny. Twenty-six miles! I'm in awe. The most I do is bike to campus on my Cannondale.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That yellow bike of yours? I see it flying down the street every day. You ride that thing to UT year-round.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: It's faster than the bus and way cheaper than a parking pass. Plus campus parking is a nightmare.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Smart. Hey, do you want some chrysanthemum tea? I just brewed a pot. We could sit on my porch for a bit.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I'd love that. I need a break from staring at survey data anyway.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Thesis stress? Bring your laptop over if you want. Sometimes a change of scenery helps.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You know what, I might just do that. Thanks, Jenny. Best next-door neighbor ever.

sessions.setting: After Sunday service at First United Methodist Church on East 12th Street

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Beautiful service today, Jenny. Pastor Williams really outdid himself with that sermon on community.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: It was lovely. I always feel recharged after our Sunday mornings here at First United Methodist. You know, the East 12th Street location just feels like home.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: It does. Emeka and I started coming here in eighty-six. Feels like the church has been woven into every chapter of my life.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Speaking of chapters, how's your memoir coming along?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Slowly but surely. I'm working on the section about Lagos in the seventies — the oil boom years. My father worked at the refinery, and the whole city felt electric with possibility. It's hard to capture that energy in words.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I bet. You should read some of it at book club sometime. We'd all love to hear it.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Maybe I will. That reminds me — for next month's book club, I was thinking about revisiting 'Things Fall Apart.' It's my favorite book, and I think Hana hasn't read it yet.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Achebe is wonderful. I'd read it again happily. Oh, by the way, I just finished my yoga teacher training! Two hundred hours at Black Swan Yoga. Got my certificate last week.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Jenny, congratulations! That's a real achievement. Are you going to teach classes?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I'm thinking about offering a free session at the garden pavilion. Maybe combine it with some herbal tea afterward.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: The gardeners would love that. You always find the most wonderful ways to bring people together.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I learned from the best — you started the whole garden, after all!

sessions.setting: At Ruth's yellow Craftsman bungalow on East 7th Street, preparing for book club

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Come in, come in! I'm just setting up the living room for Thursday's book club. Help me move these chairs?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Of course. I love this house, Ruth. The Craftsman details are beautiful.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Thank you, sweetheart. Emeka and I bought this place in 1990 for sixty-seven thousand dollars. Can you imagine? The whole block was different then.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Sixty-seven thousand! In East Austin, on 7th Street. That's unreal by today's prices.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: The neighborhood has changed a lot, but the bones of this house are still solid. So, first Thursday of every month — you're coming to book club this time, right?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Wouldn't miss it. I've been coming every month since September. Jenny's coming too, right?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Jenny hasn't missed one in two years. She's our most reliable member after you. I was thinking about suggesting 'Things Fall Apart' for April.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Oh, I've been wanting to read that! Hey, speaking of good news — I got the research grant I applied for.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Hana! Tell me everything.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: It's thirty-five hundred dollars from the UT School of Architecture. It'll fund the fieldwork for my thesis — interviews, surveys, all the community engagement stuff.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: I'm so proud of you. Your parents must be thrilled.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Mom cried. Dad said he always knew his daughter would get paid to talk to people.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Ha! That sounds like Dimitar. Now help me pick out which tea set to use. Jenny always notices these things.

sessions.setting: At the community garden, Sam working on the irrigation system

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Sam, what's all this PVC and tubing? Are you rebuilding the irrigation again?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Just upgrading the drip system. I found some recycled materials at the ReStore on Burleson — got the whole setup for about a hundred and twenty bucks.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: A hundred and twenty! That's incredible. You've always been so resourceful. I suppose growing up in Montopolis teaches you to make the most of what you've got.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ha, definitely. Montopolis wasn't exactly flush with gardening budgets. But you know, being the first person in my family to go to college — at UT, getting my math degree in 2018 — it taught me that you don't need fancy to get the job done.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Your mother must have been so proud. You earned every bit of that degree.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: She still has the diploma framed in her living room. But hey, speaking of resourceful — how are the beehives doing?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Thriving! Both hives are active. I taught myself beekeeping back in 2021, and honestly it's been one of the most rewarding things I've done at the garden. The bees help with pollination across everyone's plots.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: I've noticed. My pepper yields have been way up since you brought the bees in. Hey, did you ever hear back about this year's Travis County Fair?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Not yet, but I'm entering again. After winning first place for my Cherokee Purples last September, I feel like I have a reputation to defend.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Back-to-back champion! I'll be your hype man at the fair.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Deal. Now come over here and show me how this new drip system works. I want to make sure my tomatoes get the royal treatment.

sessions.setting: At Jenny's community acupuncture clinic event at the garden pavilion

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Okay, that's patient number twenty-five. Can you hand me another set of needles from the blue case?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Here you go. Jenny, this turnout is incredible. There's still a line outside the pavilion.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I know! I was hoping for maybe fifteen people, but we're already past twenty-five. I think we'll treat close to thirty by the end of the day.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Your Jade Wellness clinic reputation precedes you. People on Cesar Chavez already love you.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That's sweet. I've been wanting to do a free community clinic for ages. It took me years to build Jade Wellness, but giving back like this is why I got into acupuncture in the first place.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Where did you study, again? Somewhere here in Austin?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: The Academy of Oriental Medicine at Austin. Got my Master of Acupuncture in 2012. It was intense — three years of study. But it changed my life.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Clearly. Oh, by the way, I set up my bouquet table near the entrance. I've been cutting sunflowers and zinnias from my plot all morning.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Your flowers are gorgeous! Are you selling them?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Eight dollars a bouquet, same as at the SFC Farmers Market. A few people already bought some on their way in.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Smart. I should do the same with my lavender and chamomile. I've got so much growing in my garden plot right now — echinacea and lemon balm too.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You could do herbal bouquets! People would eat that up.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That's actually a brilliant idea. Let me finish up here — I think we'll hit twenty-eight patients by closing. Not bad for a Saturday at the garden!

sessions.setting: At Bennu Coffee, their regular Sunday morning planning session

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Sam! Is that a dog under the table?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Meet Gol! I adopted him from Austin Pets Alive back in January. He's a beagle mix. Named him Gol because — well, soccer.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Oh my god, he's adorable. I got a pet too — a gray cat named Banitsa. Adopted her from Austin Animal Center in February.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Banitsa? Like the Bulgarian pastry?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Exactly! She's flaky and layered, just like the real thing. Does Gol like your duplex? I imagine a beagle needs some yard space.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: My place on East 5th is small, but it's only two blocks from the garden, so I take him there all the time. He loves sniffing around the compost bins.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Ha! Okay, garden business. I pushed some updates to the website and scheduling app this week. Fixed the bug where people couldn't see their plot assignments on mobile.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Oh nice, you built that whole thing in React and Firebase, right? It's been a game-changer for scheduling.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Yeah, it was a fun side project. I'm going to add a watering reminder feature next. What else is on the agenda?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: I need to figure out a Saturday schedule for my tutoring program at Terrazas Branch Library. Some of the neighborhood kids have finals coming up, and I want to add extra sessions.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: That free tutoring program is so great, Sam. How many kids are coming regularly now?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: About twelve regulars, but a few more trickle in around test time. I just want to make sure they have the support. Nobody had that for me growing up.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You're making such a difference. Okay, let me pull up the garden schedule and we can sort out the rest.

sessions.setting: Walking to their cars after Sunday church service

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Jenny, do you need a ride? I'm parked right over there — the white RAV4.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Thanks, Ruth, but I drove today. My blue Tucson's just around the corner. David needed me to pick up the twins after this.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: How are Lily and Rose doing?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Busy as always. Hey, I wanted to tell you — Pastor Williams mentioned the Capital Area Food Bank needs volunteers for their summer drive.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Oh, I've been meaning to reconnect with them. Last year we donated two hundred pounds of produce from the garden. It felt wonderful to see it go to people who needed it.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That's incredible. I donated some herbal tea blends to their holiday gift basket program back in December. It's such a good organization.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: We should coordinate a garden donation again this fall. Speaking of volunteering, I've got my literacy program at the Austin Public Library on Wednesday afternoon, so I'll be busy midweek.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Every Wednesday, like clockwork. You really don't stop, do you, Ruth?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Retirement doesn't mean resting! The kids at the library need reading support, and it keeps my mind sharp. After thirty-two years as a librarian, I can't exactly stop caring about literacy.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That's what I love about you. Okay, I need to run. See you at the garden this week?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: I'll be there Saturday for sure. I'm making pepper soup, as always. Bring the girls — I'll save them some.

sessions.setting: At the community garden during a Saturday morning work session

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Sam! Congratulations! I heard about Teacher of the Year at Travis High!

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Thanks, Jenny! They announced it Friday at the awards assembly. I'm still kind of in shock.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Sam, I'm not shocked at all. You teach AP Calc and Algebra II, you coach the girls' soccer team to the district semifinals, and you tutor on weekends. Who else could it be?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: The soccer season was wild this year. Getting to the district semifinals — the girls worked so hard. I'm really proud of them.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: And didn't you just finish your master's degree too?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Yeah, got my M.Ed. from Texas State back in December. It was a long haul doing it while teaching full-time, but worth it.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: A master's degree and Teacher of the Year in the same school year. Sam, you need to slow down and eat some pepper soup. Come, I made a big pot this morning.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ruth, your Saturday pepper soup is sacred. I'd never say no.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Save me a bowl too! I'm heading out soon — I'm teaching a workshop on growing medicinal herbs at the Austin Garden Center this afternoon.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: That's today? Break a leg, Jenny.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Thanks! I've been prepping slides all week. I'm covering everything from lavender propagation to lemon balm tinctures. Wish me luck!

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: You'll be great. Save us some samples?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Always. Okay, pepper soup first, then I'm off.

sessions.setting: At Jenny's house, over the fence while Jenny is gardening in her yard

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Hey Jenny! I can hear Lily and Rose playing in your backyard. Sounds like a party over there.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: They're practicing for their school talent show. Seventh graders with big dreams — Kealing Middle School won't know what hit them.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: That's adorable. How's David handling the noise?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: He's at the office. Saturday overtime at Kimley-Horn — they're pushing to finish a bridge design. Structural engineering waits for no one, apparently.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I get it. My dad's the same way with his garage. Petrov's Garage on East Riverside — he works six days a week. My mom keeps telling him to slow down.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Your mom is the folk dance teacher, right? At the Bulgarian Cultural Center?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: That's her! Irina Petrov, teaching Bulgarian folk dance to anyone who'll listen. She tried to get me to perform at the spring recital, but I have two left feet.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Ha! I'd love to see a Bulgarian folk dance sometime. I keep telling Lily and Rose they should try different cultural dances. Expose them to more than just what they see in Austin.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Do you ever take them to Houston to visit your mom's restaurant?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Oh, all the time. My mother, Mei-Ling, owns Lucky Star in Chinatown. Best dim sum in Houston. She spoils the twins rotten every time we visit.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I need to go! I've always wanted to try authentic dim sum.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Next time we drive down, you should come. I'll translate the menu for you — Mandarin, Cantonese, English, I've got you covered. I speak all three fluently.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Deal! And I'll teach you how to say 'delicious' in Bulgarian in return.

sessions.setting: At the community garden, Hana interviewing Ruth for her thesis

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Okay Ruth, I'm recording now. For the thesis interview — can you tell me about your background and how you got involved with the garden?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Of course. Well, I was born in Lagos, Nigeria, and I moved to Austin in 1985 to attend the University of Texas. I was twenty-four years old with a suitcase and a dream of becoming a librarian.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: And you did become one — at Zavala Elementary, right?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Thirty-two years as the school librarian. Retired in 2017. The garden started the year after, partly because I needed something to pour my energy into.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I can relate to Austin roots. I was born right here — my parents emigrated from Sofia, Bulgaria, in ninety-five. So Austin is the only home I've ever known.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: It's a special city. When Emeka and I settled in East Austin, it was a very different place. He was a civil engineering professor at UT. We built a whole life here.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I'm so sorry about his passing. When was that?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: 2019. It was sudden — a heart attack. But the garden was already going by then, and this community kept me afloat. The neighbors, the church, all of it.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: That's exactly the kind of resilience my thesis is trying to document. Community spaces as support systems.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: You understand it because you've lived it, Hana. Now tell me, didn't you do some work with the city before graduate school?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I interned at the Austin City Planning Department the summer of 2023. I worked on the East Riverside corridor plan. That experience is actually what pushed me to focus my thesis on East Austin.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: East Riverside has changed so much. Good that they had someone who actually knows the area working on it.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Thank you, Ruth. This interview is gold. I'll transcribe it this weekend.

sessions.setting: At the community garden potluck organized by Sam

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: I can't believe forty-five people showed up! I was hoping for twenty, maybe thirty.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Sam, you basically invited the entire neighborhood. What did you expect? Also, those birria tacos are unreal. What's your secret?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: My grandmother Lupe's recipe. She taught me when I was twelve. Slow-braised beef cheeks, her special chili blend — it's the only dish I cook that I'd put up against a restaurant.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: They're delicious, Sam. Almost as good as my pepper soup. Almost.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ha! High praise from you, Ruth. Hey, is that the band setting up over there?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Wait, did you get Los Relámpagos to play at the potluck?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Well, I play guitar in Los Relámpagos, so I just told the guys to show up. We usually play at Sahara Lounge on East 6th, but a garden gig sounded fun.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: A live Tejano band at our garden potluck! Sam, this is wonderful. I need to call Adaeze and tell her about this — she's always saying East Austin is losing its character.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Tell your daughter to come visit! Oh, I almost forgot — Sam, I was at Veracruz All Natural this morning for my usual Saturday migas taco, and I ran into three people who said they were coming to the potluck.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: That place is your second home, I swear.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Sam, before you go play, come try this jollof rice I brought. I made it special for today — Igbo-style. You know I speak Igbo and Yoruba along with English, so I've got recipes from both sides.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ruth, you could open a restaurant with your cooking. Okay, let me grab a plate and then I've got to go tune up. This potluck is officially a party!

sessions.setting: At Ruth's house after book club, cleaning up

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Good discussion tonight. I think 'Things Fall Apart' really resonated with the group.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: It always does. Here, have some of this tea while we clean up. Is this your chrysanthemum blend?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Yes! My hand-blended chrysanthemum and goji berry mix. I source the chrysanthemum from a farm in Fujian province — my cousin connects me directly with the grower.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: It's lovely. So tell me, when did you move to Austin again? I always forget the exact year.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: 2010. Born and raised in Houston, but David's job brought us here, and I fell in love with East Austin immediately. Opened Jade Wellness two years later.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Fourteen years already. You've become such a fixture in this community. Remember when you planted that fig tree at the garden entrance?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: October 2023! That little sapling is fifteen feet tall now. The shade it throws over the picnic area makes the summer potlucks bearable.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Sam's potluck earlier this month was proof of that. Everyone was sitting under your fig tree eating birria tacos.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Ha! That was a great day. Hey, how's Adaeze doing? Is she still swamped with cases?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Always. Immigration law in Houston is never slow. She's handling three asylum cases right now. And Chidi is buried in code at Dell up in Round Rock. My children work too hard.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: They take after their mother. An immigration lawyer and a software engineer — you and Emeka raised them right.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Thank you, Jenny. Now let me wrap up some of this food for Lily and Rose. Growing girls need to eat.

sessions.setting: At the community garden, both watering their plots in the early morning to beat the Texas heat

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Sam! You're here early. It's not even seven.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: July in Austin — if I don't water before eight, the sun will cook everything. My peppers are already struggling.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Smart. I did my Lady Bird Lake run at six fifteen, then came straight here. My herbs need morning water in this heat. How's school? Wait, school's out, right?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Summer break, thank God. AP Calc and Algebra II all year long takes it out of you. But I've still got summer soccer camp for the girls' team.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: You never stop. David's the same way — his mom always says he needs to rest. Speaking of family, how's your mom doing?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: She's good. Working hard as always at CommUnityCare on East Cesar Chavez. Being a medical assistant during summer means flu's down but heat exhaustion cases are up.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Oh, I know that clinic! Some of my patients go there. Tell Elena I said hi.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Will do. ¿Le digo en español o inglés? Mom prefers Spanish, but she switches back and forth.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I wish I spoke Spanish! I've got Mandarin, Cantonese, and English, but my Spanish is limited to ordering at taco trucks.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ha! Well, growing up bilingual in East Austin was just how it was. Hey, have you met my sister Rosa? She's a nurse at Seton Medical Center. I keep trying to get her to come to the garden.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: A nurse! My mother would approve. She always wanted me to go into traditional medicine. Well, I guess acupuncture counts.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Counts double, I'd say. Oh, the drip timer just clicked on — let me check the emitters on Ruth's side of the bed.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I'll finish up here and head out. My nine o'clock patient is coming to the clinic. See you at the garden meeting tomorrow?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: I'll be there. Stay cool out there, Jenny.

sessions.setting: Walking through the community garden after their Sunday coffee meeting

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Hey, is that your car? The red Civic?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Yep, my trusty 2016 Honda Civic. Got ninety-seven thousand miles on it. She's hanging in there, but I might need to take her to your dad's shop soon. Something's rattling under the hood.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Bring it to Petrov's Garage on East Riverside! Dad will take care of you. He gives all the garden people a discount.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: For real? I'll swing by this week then. Oh, how was your Habitat for Humanity build yesterday?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Exhausting but awesome. Second Saturday of the month, every month. We're framing a house over in Del Valle right now. I love it.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: You do so much community stuff on top of grad school. How do you manage it all?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Honestly, I don't know. My Spanish helps sometimes — a lot of the Habitat volunteers are Spanish-speaking, and my intermediate Spanish is enough to get by on a construction site.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Wait, you speak Spanish? Since when?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I'm not fluent like you. It's intermediate — I took it all through high school and college. Plus Bulgarian and English, obviously. Growing up in East Austin, you pick up a lot of Spanish just from the neighborhood.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Trilingual! Impressive. My sunflowers look great today, by the way. Your plot is really coming together.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Thanks! I sold ten bouquets at the farmers market yesterday. Oh, I was at Veracruz All Natural for my Saturday migas taco and someone asked if I do wedding flowers. Can you imagine?

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Hana Petrov: urban planner, flower vendor, wedding florist. The side hustles are multiplying.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: One thing at a time! Let me finish this thesis first.

sessions.setting: Community garden mural-painting day organized by Hana

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Everybody, the artist is here! Maria Torres just pulled up with all her paint supplies. The mural wall is prepped and ready.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Hana, you really pulled this together beautifully. How big is the mural going to be?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Twelve by eight feet. Maria's designing it around the theme of community growth — flowers, vegetables, hands working together. She's a local artist from the Eastside.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: This is awesome. I asked my Los Relámpagos bandmates if they wanted to come help paint, and three of them said yes.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: The more hands the better! I brought some lemon balm lemonade from my garden herbs. And lavender shortbread cookies.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: And I've got my Saturday pepper soup warming on the camp stove over there. We'll need it once people get hungry.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Ruth's pepper soup and Jenny's herb lemonade — this is the best-catered painting event in Austin history.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Maria wants volunteers to help with the background colors first. She'll do the detailed work herself. Who's grabbing a brush?

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: I'll take a brush! I might be sixty-three, but I can still paint a wall.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Count me in too. Let me set down this tray of chamomile and echinacea seedlings I brought for people to take home.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Perfect. Okay everyone, let's make some art! This mural is going to be the first thing people see when they walk into the garden.

sessions.setting: At the community garden, harvesting tomatoes from their shared bed

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Look at these Brandywines, Sam. They're perfect. And the Cherokee Purples are even bigger than last year's fair winners.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: You're going to sweep the Travis County Fair again. Last September's first place was just the beginning.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: I've been growing fourteen varieties in our shared bed now, and every single one produced this year. The drip system you built really helped.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: That's the magic of this twenty-by-forty raised bed — plenty of room for your tomatoes and enough sun exposure on the south side.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: The bees helped too. Both my hives have been incredibly active this summer. The pollination has been fantastic across the whole garden.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Tell me about it — my Carolina Reapers are the biggest they've ever been. Same with the habaneros. I've got more peppers than I know what to do with.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Make hot sauce! You could sell it at the farmers market alongside Hana's flower bouquets.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Don't tempt me. Actually, that's not a bad idea. 'Delgado's Death Sauce.' Has a ring to it.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Ha! Just don't put it in my pepper soup. I like it hot, but Carolina Reaper hot might send me to the hospital.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Deal. Let me fill up another basket — we should have enough to donate a big batch to the food bank this year.

sessions.setting: At Ruth's house during book club, discussing Hana's upcoming conference presentation

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Before we start tonight's book discussion, can we all congratulate Hana? Tell them your news, sweetheart.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I got accepted to present at the American Planning Association's Texas Chapter conference in October!

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Hana! That's incredible! What are you presenting?

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: My green space research — basically a preview of my thesis findings. I'm a second-year master's student presenting alongside practicing planners with decades of experience. I'm terrified.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: Don't you dare be terrified. Your thesis on community-led green spaces as catalysts for neighborhood resilience is important work. Those planners need to hear from someone who actually lives in the community they're studying.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Ruth's right. I've been coming to this book club on the first Thursday of every month for two years, and in that time I've watched you grow from a nervous grad student into a real researcher.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You both are going to make me cry. The book club has honestly been one of the best parts of my week. Ruth hosting us here every month — it's exactly the kind of community connection my thesis is about.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: This Eastside Book Club started as just me and two neighbors in 2019. Now we have twelve regulars. Community grows when you give it space.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That should be a quote in your presentation, Hana. Straight from the co-founder of the garden herself.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: I'm actually going to use our garden as a case study. The survey data, Ruth's interview, the mural day — it all ties together.

turns.speaker: Ruth Okonkwo
turns.text: We're proud of you. Now, let's get to the book. Jenny, did you finish this month's selection?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Read it twice! Let's discuss.

sessions.setting: At Bennu Coffee celebrating Hana's conference presentation, after her return

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: To Hana — our very own conference presenter! Bennu Coffee has never seen this much celebration on a Sunday morning.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: You guys didn't have to do this. It's supposed to be our regular planning session, Sam!

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Our Sunday morning coffee meetings can handle one week of celebration. Tell us everything about the APA Texas conference.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: It was amazing. My session had about sixty people. I presented all the findings from my East Austin green space research, and three different city planners came up afterward asking for my contact info.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: That's networking gold. I'm so proud of you. I biked over here to celebrate — well, I drove actually, but normally I would have run. I'm trying to save my legs for marathon training.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: How's the Austin Marathon training going?

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I'm up to sixteen miles on my long runs. February is going to come fast, but I think I'll be ready for my first full marathon.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Jenny running a marathon, Hana presenting at conferences — I need to step up my game. Maybe I'll enter a hot pepper eating contest.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: With those Carolina Reapers you grow, you'd win for sure. Oh, and I biked to the conference center on my yellow Cannondale, by the way. The valet parking guys had no idea what to do with a bicycle.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: Classic Hana. Riding your hybrid bike in professional attire. I love it.

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Okay, let's do some actual garden planning too. We need to talk about fall planting and the end-of-season harvest festival.

turns.speaker: Hana Petrov
turns.text: Right, business as usual. I'll pull up the scheduling app. But first — another round of lattes. My treat.

turns.speaker: Jenny Liu
turns.text: I'll take an oat milk cortado. Cheers to Hana!

turns.speaker: Sam Delgado
turns.text: Cheers!
